newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain's privatisation drive switches into high gear.
newsitem.headline: Spain's privatisation drive switches into high gear.

text.p: Spain boosted its privatisation drive late on Tuesday by closing the sale on two state-owned metals producers, considered less attractive than the crown jewels sold up until now.
Deals for two metals groups -- steel company Corporacion Siderurgica Integral (CSI) and aluminium manufacturer Inespal -- were clinched on Tuesday.

"Now the process (of privatisation) has picked up pace. We are going to continue down this road because I think it's what this country needs and it has been well-received by the markets," Industry Minister Josep Pique said after the signings.

Luxembourg steel maker Arbed won 35-percent of CSI over a French rival. It will subscribe a capital increase of 129 billion pesetas. CSI will in turn invest some 100 billion pesetas of that amount in stakes in Arbed group companies.
And, despite last minute haggling, Spain also sold aluminium producer Inespal to Aluminum Co of America (Alcoa) for 61.5 billion pesetas.

"Rather than good news for the companies it's good news for the government -- being able to sell Repsol and Telefonica is not amazing because they are two good companies but selling CIS and Inespal is," a metals company analyst at a Spanish brokerage said.
Spain's one-year-old conservative government, eager to slim down the state, has pursued privatisations aggressively.

This year alone it has sold 10 percent of top energy group Repsol and 20 percent of top telecommunications group Telefonica TEL.MC. Both were rousing successes. Its biggest privatisation yet, of utility Endesa, is coming up this autumn.
But where both Telefonica and Repsol were already partly public, CSI and Inespal have been sheltered from the tough competition the others have faced.

Alcoa has pledged to invest an additional 65 billion pesetas in the financially troubled Inespal, which has racked up losses of more than 67 billion pesetas since 1990 despite turning a profit in the last two years.
As part of the deal, Inespal will retain its privileged electrical rates, a form of state subsidy, an analyst said. The group, a heavy consumer, pays about half the going rate.
"If you're selling a company which is receiving subsidies you're probably not selling a company that is competitive," the analyst said.
But the government has repeatedly stated its will to sell its less competitive groups as soon as possible.

"It certainly gives one the sense that there are going to be more privatisations," said Alfredo Urrutia, chief economist at Societe Generale in Madrid. "It's part of their idea of taking apart the state -- they want it considerably smaller."

The news is clearly good for the two groups. Both deals secure jobs, provide for fresh investments, and vault them into the big leagues, internationally, in their respective businesses, analysts said.
"CSI and Inespal are now in the hands of the main players in the market," said a Madrid-based analyst.

Through the deal, CSI becomes Europe's biggest iron and steel group and the third biggest in the world. For its part Inespal, will represent half of the European aluminium production of Alcoa, the largest world producer.
